blocks.content: This new module turns to a genuinely important, practical question: HTTP, exactly as covered throughout the entire previous module, is built around the client always asking first, with the server only ever responding. But what happens when a client genuinely needs to know about something the moment it happens on the server, a new chat message, a live score update, without the server ever being able to reach out on its own?

Polling is the simplest possible answer to this problem, and understanding its real strengths and honest weaknesses sets up every other topic in this module, each one a genuine improvement addressing a specific limitation polling has.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017466782-248658600.png
blocks.alt: Polling: the client repeatedly asks the server whether anything new has happened, using ordinary HTTP requests

blocks.content: 1. The Core Constraint: The Server Can Never Just Push
blocks.text: 1. The Core Constraint: The Server Can Never Just Push

blocks.content: Recall from the http-basics topic that HTTP strictly follows a request and response model, the client always initiates, the server only ever responds. This means a server genuinely cannot spontaneously send a client new information the moment it becomes available, no matter how badly the application might want that.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017468701-95393646.png
blocks.alt: Plain HTTP requires the client to always ask first, the server can never spontaneously push new data on its own

blocks.content: 2. Polling: The Simplest Possible Workaround

Polling works around this constraint in the most direct way imaginable: the client simply asks repeatedly, on a fixed timer, is there anything new yet, using perfectly ordinary HTTP requests. If nothing has changed, the server responds saying so, and the client just tries again a little later.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017470205-744096708.png
blocks.alt: On a fixed timer, the client repeatedly sends ordinary HTTP requests asking whether anything new has happened

blocks.content: 3. The Real, Honest Cost: Wasted Requests
blocks.text: 3. The Real, Honest Cost: Wasted Requests

blocks.content: The overwhelming majority of polling requests, in most real applications, find absolutely nothing new to report at all. Every single one of those empty checks is still a real HTTP request, a real TCP round trip, real server processing, genuinely wasted effort for zero actual benefit.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017471766-762961435.png
blocks.alt: Most polling requests find nothing new, representing real, honestly wasted server load and network traffic

blocks.title: This is not a hypothetical inefficiency
blocks.content: At real scale, with many clients all polling simultaneously, this wasted load adds up to a genuinely significant, measurable cost on server infrastructure, not just a minor theoretical concern.
4. The Interval Tradeoff

Choosing how often to poll is a genuine, honest tradeoff with no universally correct answer. A short polling interval delivers fresher, more up to date data, at the cost of far more wasted requests. A long polling interval wastes fewer requests, but data can be noticeably stale for a real stretch of time between checks.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017473254-742783518.png
blocks.alt: A short interval means fresher data but more waste; a long interval means less waste but noticeably staler data

5. A Real World Analogy

Walking to check your physical mailbox every single hour, whether or not anything has actually arrived, captures polling exactly. It is simple, and it works, but most trips find the mailbox completely empty, real effort spent for no actual result, purely because you had no way of knowing in advance whether it was actually worth checking.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017474786-542019125.png
blocks.alt: Checking your mailbox every hour regardless of whether anything arrived captures exactly what polling does

blocks.content: 6. When Polling Is Actually a Perfectly Fine Choice
blocks.text: 6. When Polling Is Actually a Perfectly Fine Choice

blocks.content: For data that genuinely changes rarely, or where some real delay before seeing an update is genuinely acceptable, polling is a perfectly reasonable, simple, easy to implement choice, its simplicity is a real, honest advantage in exactly these cases. For data that changes constantly, needing genuinely near instant updates, polling starts to feel wasteful and laggy at the same time.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017476298-457889349.png
blocks.alt: Polling is genuinely fine for infrequently changing data; it becomes wasteful and laggy for data needing near instant updates

7. Where This Module Goes Next

The rest of this module covers three genuinely different improvements on plain polling, each one addressing its real limitations in a different way: long polling, server sent events, and websockets. Each of them is worth understanding specifically in contrast to the wasted request and staleness tradeoffs covered in this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784017477920-612782286.png
blocks.alt: Long polling, server sent events, and websockets each improve on polling honest limitations in a genuinely different way

blocks.title: Keep this topic in mind as a baseline
blocks.content: Every technique covered in the rest of this module is genuinely best understood as a direct answer to a specific weakness of plain polling covered here, wasted requests, or staleness, or both.
